title: Pairing weave
subtitle: The two-rod foundation weave for basket bases and sides
excerpt: Pairing is the weave used to build the base of almost every British willow basket. Two rods work alternately, each passing in front of one stake and behind the next, twisting around each other between stakes. The twist locks the stakes in position and produces a dense, even weave.

glossaryTerms.definition: A two-rod weave in which two weavers alternate, each passing in front of one stake and behind the next, with a half-twist between stakes that locks the rods together.
The thinner rods woven between the stakes to build up the sides of the basket.
The upright structural rods of a basket that form the frame for the woven sides. Stakes are heavier-gauge rods than weavers.

content.text: Pairing is a two-rod weave: two weavers alternate around the
stake

s, each passing in front of one stake and behind the next, with a half-twist between each stake that crosses the two rods over each other. The crossing-over is what gives the weave its name and its structural property. The crossed weavers grip each stake between them, which is why
pairing
is the foundation weave for bases and for any part of the basket where the stakes need to be locked in a fixed position.
Setting up
Insert two
weavers

into the work. On a slath base, slide both weavers side by side into the same gap alongside one of the base sticks. On a sided basket, insert them into adjacent spaces between stakes. The butt ends go in first for the start of a weaver; tips are joined in when the rod runs out.
The stroke
Take the left-hand weaver (the one behind the current stake) and bring it forward over the right-hand weaver.
Pass it in front of the next stake to the right.
Take it behind the following stake and out to the front again.
The weaver now sits behind the new 'current' stake. The rods have swapped sides.
Repeat: take the new left-hand weaver forward, in front of the next stake, behind the next, out.
Joining in

When a weaver runs out, join in a new one at the tip end (thinner end) of the old weaver. Lay the new weaver's butt end alongside the old tip for four stakes, then pull the old tip out and continue with the new. Joining at tips and butts alternately keeps the weave level: a butt-to-butt join in the same place on two adjacent weavers would create a lump.
Common errors

Taking the wrong rod first: if the back rod is not taken forward each time, the twist is lost and the weave becomes a simple plain weave with no locking action. The rule is always: take the back rod forward first.
Uneven tension: each weaver should pull to the same tightness. Loose pairing leaves gaps that collapse under load. Use the rapping iron to bed the rounds down evenly after every three rounds.
Joining both rods at the same place: stagger the joins so that two new butts do not appear at the same stake in the same round. This keeps the weave level and the basket round.
Where pairing is used
The base of all round and oval baskets using a slath construction.
The sides of any basket where a dense, tight weave is preferred over the more open randing.
The first few rounds of any sided section, to lock the stakes in position before switching to a faster weave.
